I found 19 households to call. Five took a backdoor Roth that is partly taxable, ten had a 2025 RMD that wasn't taken, and four had a wash sale. None is left unresolved.

**1. Backdoor Roth partly taxable (5 households).** Each person put a nondeductible 2025 contribution into a new traditional IRA and converted it. But each also still had a pre-tax rollover IRA on 31 Dec 2025, so the pro-rata rule makes about 96–97% of each conversion taxable. Their IRA basis was $0 at the end of 2024, so the 2025 contribution is their only basis.

| Household | Person | Conversion | Rollover IRA at 31 Dec 2025 | Taxable (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HH-0690 | Nadia Brannigan | $8,000 | $187,878.56 | $7,673 |
| HH-0218 | Yusuf Rasmussen | $7,000 | $221,659.62 | $6,786 |
| HH-0347 | Hana Yamaguchi | $7,000 | $231,265.99 | $6,794 |
| HH-1204 | Luka Kovac | $7,000 | $187,544.92 | $6,748 |
| HH-0844 | Anders Moreau | $7,000 | $152,329.55 | $6,692 |

The other five backdoor households (HH-0799, 1587, 0608, 0747, 0633) are fine: their pre-tax money is in a 401(k), which the pro-rata rule ignores.

**2. RMD not met, 401(k) (5 households).** Each client was born in 1952, so 2025 was their first RMD year, due by 1 April 2026. Each signed one payment from an IRA equal to the RMD of all their retirement accounts added together, including the 401(k). The amounts match those totals divided by 26.5. A 401(k)'s RMD can't be taken from an IRA, so each 401(k)'s RMD is still unpaid and the deadline has passed:
- HH-0120 Laila Udeh: about $12,582
- HH-0371 Rosa Tamura: about $15,164
- HH-0664 Freya Chaudhry: about $11,020
- HH-5271 Teodoro Villanueva: about $12,730
- HH-0236 Xavier Santangelo: about $10,956

**3. RMD not met, inherited IRA (5 households).** In each case the prior custodian confirms the parent who died had already started taking RMDs. A non-spouse child inheriting in that case must take a yearly RMD from 2025 on. None of these inherited IRAs paid anything out in 2025: HH-0466, HH-0607, HH-0491, HH-0842 and HH-7126.

The five inherited IRAs where the parent had not started RMDs (HH-0716, 0571, 0330, 0328, 7683) owe no yearly RMD.

**4. Wash sales (4 households).** Each couple sold a fund at a loss in their joint taxable account. Within 30 days, the same fund was bought in one spouse's IRA or Roth IRA. Because the replacement shares are in a retirement account, the disallowed part of the loss is lost for good.

| Household | Fund | Loss | Replacement | Disallowed (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HH-0363 | Brackwater Dividend Equity Fund | $35,820.62 | 1,340 shares, 13 days later | $15,037 |
| HH-0780 | Larkspur Developed Markets Fund | $12,860.65 | 390 shares, 28 days later | $5,706 |
| HH-9234 | Wexcombe Mid Cap Fund | $53,516.17 | 500 shares, 16 days later | $31,592 |
| HH-0129 | Wexcombe Mid Cap Fund | $31,896.36 | 360 shares, 12 days later (Roth IRA) | $17,886 |

Six other loss sales fall just outside the window, between 31 and 41 days: HH-0380, 0847, 0981, 9571, 0679 and 0221.

**Checks that cleared other households:**
- The other 2025 RMDs, including the ones that used charitable distributions, match the 31 Dec 2024 balances divided by the IRS table factor for the owner's age.
- For stock-award shares the custodian shows with no cost basis, the true basis is the share price on the vesting date in the CRM notes. That shows they are either gains, or losses with no repurchase within 30 days.

**Outside the three kinds, but worth knowing:**
- Four charitable distribution requests (HH-0190, 0445, 6047, 0782) were paid out as ordinary distributions.
- Four ordinary Roth conversions (HH-0404, 0287, 4633, 0616) rely on nondeductible basis that has no Form 8606 on file.

arguments:
You are helping an advisor at a small independent advisory firm. This folder holds the records of every client household of the firm as they stood on 15 April 2026, one folder per household under households/<household ID>/, each with the custodian's files (custodian/), the firm's portfolio system (portfolio/) and its CRM (crm/).

The advisor asks: which households should we call before 15 April 2026 about a 2025 tax or distribution surprise, and why?

Count three kinds of surprise, and no other:
- "backdoor_roth_taxed": a 2025 contribution to a traditional IRA converted to a Roth IRA in 2025, part of which is taxable under the pro-rata rule because the person's traditional IRAs held pre-tax money on 31 December 2025;
- "rmd_not_met": a 2025 required minimum distribution, from any retirement account, that was not met;
- "wash_sale": a 2025 sale at a loss in a taxable account, with the same security acquired within 30 days before or after it in an account of the seller or the seller's spouse, so that some of the loss is a wash sale.

Work only from these files. End your answer with one fenced json block with these fields:
- "finding": "found" if one or more households had such a surprise, "none_found" if none did, or "unresolved" if the files settle no household as found and leave some unresolved
- "households": one entry per household to call, each as {"household_id": ..., "surprises": the kinds above that apply, "person_ids": the person each surprise concerns (who converted, whose RMD was not met), "account_ids": the accounts an unmet RMD had to come from, "transaction_ids": the backdoor Roth's conversion, and the wash sale's loss sales and the acquisitions that replace them, "explanation": one sentence}, or [] if none
- "unresolved": the households the files cannot settle, each as {"household_id": ..., "explanation": one sentence}, or [] if none
- "figures": every figure you relied on from the files, each as {"label": ..., "value": ..., "source": the file it came from, relative to this folder}, adding "computed": true to a figure you computed from them rather than read
- "explanation": two or three sentences
